concept.title: Sum of digits of 1/p for half-period length and p ≡ 1 mod 4
concept.concept_description: Let p be a prime, b an integer ≥ 2 such that p does not divide b. If the multiplicative order of b modulo p is (p-1)/2, and p ≡ 1 mod 4, then the sum of the digits of one period of the base-b expansion of 1/p is (b-1)(p-1)/4.
concept.mathematical_framing: Let p be a prime, b an integer ≥ 2 such that p does not divide b. If the multiplicative order of b modulo p is (p-1)/2, and p ≡ 1 mod 4, then the sum of the digits of one period of the base-b expansion of 1/p is (b-1)(p-1)/4.
concept.lean_guess: Define the sequence of digits in the base-b expansion of 1/p. Show that they are given by the integer division of b by p times the sequence of remainders. Use the fact that the remainders cycle through the elements of the subgroup of index 2 in (Z/pZ)*. Since p ≡ 1 mod 4, -1 is in this subgroup, which implies that the digits can be paired as (d, b-1-d). The sum of each pair is b-1, and there are (p-1)/4 pairs, giving a total sum of (b-1)(p-1)/4.

concept.title: Polynomiality of Nilpotent Matrix Counts with Prescribed Support
concept.concept_description: For any partition λ of n and any support pattern S ⊆ [n] × [n], the number of n × n nilpotent matrices over F_q with Jordan canonical form type λ and support contained in S is a polynomial in q with non-negative integer coefficients. This extends known polynomiality results for Hessenberg supports (connected to chromatic quasisymmetric function evaluations via Shareshian–Wachs theory) and directly addresses the polynomiality questions the paper raises for more general support patterns and prescribed affine slices of adjoint orbits.
concept.mathematical_framing: For any partition λ of n and any support pattern S ⊆ [n] × [n], the number of n × n nilpotent matrices over F_q with Jordan canonical form type λ and support contained in S is a polynomial in q with non-negative integer coefficients. This extends known polynomiality results for Hessenberg supports (connected to chromatic quasisymmetric function evaluations via Shareshian–Wachs theory) and directly addresses the polynomiality questions the paper raises for more general support patterns and prescribed affine slices of adjoint orbits.
concept.lean_guess: Leverage the paper's Hall scalar product formula expressing the count in terms of skew modified Hall-Littlewood functions and q-Whittaker functions. For Hessenberg supports, connect to chromatic quasisymmetric functions and the Shareshian-Wachs theorem relating Hessenberg variety point counts to chromatic quasisymmetric function evaluations. For general supports, develop combinatorial-algebraic tools showing the relevant Hall scalar products specialize to polynomials in q, potentially using geometric methods on Springer fibers and deformation arguments to reduce arbitrary supports to Hessenberg-type patterns.

concept.lean_guess: Define the base-b digit sequence of 1/p using the division algorithm on remainders, a_i = ⌊b * r_i / p⌋ where r_i = b^i mod p. import Mathlib

/-!
# Latin square graphs: definition and regularity

A **Latin square** of order `n` is a function `M : Fin n → Fin n → Fin n` whose
rows and columns are each bijections of `Fin n`.  Its associated *Latin square
graph* `L(M)` has vertex set the `n²` cells `Fin n × Fin n`, and two distinct
cells are adjacent iff they share a row, share a column, or carry the same symbol.

This file develops the graph and proves the first structural fact underlying the
research target on the second clique homology of `L(M)`: **`L(M)` is regular of
degree `3(n-1)`**.  The three adjacency types (same row / same column / same
symbol) partition the neighbourhood of every cell into three blocks of size
`n-1`, which is exactly the content of `LatinSquare.neighbors_card`.

The regularity degree `3(n-1)`, together with the parameters `λ = n` and `μ = 6`,
identifies `L(M)` as a strongly regular graph `srg(n², 3(n-1), n, 6)` for `n ≥ 5`;
the clique-homology dimension formula `(n-1)³ - I(M)` is stated relative to this
graph.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer): the Latin square graph is regular, and the degree is
`3(n-1)` because a cell has exactly `n-1` co-row cells, `n-1` co-column cells, and
`n-1` co-symbol cells, and these three families are pairwise disjoint.

EXPERIMENT (Experimenter): computed the degree of the cyclic Latin square
`M i j = i + j` for `n = 2..6`, obtaining `3, 6, 9, 12, 15 = 3(n-1)`.  Formalized
the general statement by exhibiting the neighbourhood as a disjoint union of three
`image`/`filter` sets and summing their cardinalities.

ANALYSIS (Analyst): disjointness is exactly where the *Latin* property is used:
two co-row cells never share a symbol (row injectivity) and two co-column cells
never share a symbol (column injectivity); co-row and co-column cells meet only at
the base cell.  The co-symbol block has size `n-1` because each of the `n` rows
contains the fixed symbol exactly once (row bijectivity).

CRITIQUE (Critic): the statement is non-vacuous for every `n ≥ 1` (the cyclic
square witnesses existence) and the proof genuinely uses bijectivity, not a mere
counting coincidence.  Degree regularity alone does not pin down the homology, but
it is the first of the strongly-regular parameters the target formula relies on.

SYNTHESIS (PI): `L(M)` is placed on a firm combinatorial footing; regularity of
degree `3(n-1)` is proved for all Latin squares, feeding the intercalate/clique
analysis of `Intercalates.lean`.
-/

namespace LatinSquareGraph

open Finset Function

/-- A Latin square of order `n`: rows and columns are bijections of `Fin n`. -/
structure LatinSquare (n : ℕ) where
  /-- The symbol in row `r`, column `c`. -/
  M : Fin n → Fin n → Fin n
  /-- Each row is a bijection (every symbol appears once per row). -/
  row_bij : ∀ r, Bijective (M r)
  /-- Each column is a bijection (every symbol appears once per column). -/
  col_bij : ∀ c, Bijective (fun r => M r c)

variable {n : ℕ}

/-- Adjacency in the Latin square graph: distinct cells sharing a row, a column,
or a symbol. -/
def LatinSquare.Adj (L : LatinSquare n) (p q : Fin n × Fin n) : Prop :=
  p ≠ q ∧ (p.1 = q.1 ∨ p.2 = q.2 ∨ L.M p.1 p.2 = L.M q.1 q.2)

/-- The neighbourhood of a cell `p` as a finite set. -/
def LatinSquare.neighbors (L : LatinSquare n) (p : Fin n × Fin n) :
    Finset (Fin n × Fin n) :=
  univ.filter (fun q => q ≠ p ∧
    (p.1 = q.1 ∨ p.2 = q.2 ∨ L.M p.1 p.2 = L.M q.1 q.2))

/-- Cells in the same row as `p` (excluding `p`). -/
def LatinSquare.rowSet (p : Fin n × Fin n) : Finset (Fin n × Fin n) :=
  (univ.erase p.2).image (fun c => (p.1, c))

/-- Cells in the same column as `p` (excluding `p`). -/
def LatinSquare.colSet (p : Fin n × Fin n) : Finset (Fin n × Fin n) :=
  (univ.erase p.1).image (fun r => (r, p.2))

/-- Cells carrying the same symbol as `p` (excluding `p`). -/
def LatinSquare.symSet (L : LatinSquare n) (p : Fin n × Fin n) :
    Finset (Fin n × Fin n) :=
  (univ.filter (fun q => L.M q.1 q.2 = L.M p.1 p.2)).erase p

theorem LatinSquare.rowSet_card (p : Fin n × Fin n) :
    (LatinSquare.rowSet p).card = n - 1 := by
      convert Finset.card_image_of_injective _ ?_ using 1 <;> norm_num [ Function.Injective ]

theorem LatinSquare.colSet_card (p : Fin n × Fin n) :
    (LatinSquare.colSet p).card = n - 1 := by
      erw [ Finset.card_image_of_injective _ fun x y h => by injection h, Finset.card_erase_of_mem ( Finset.mem_univ _ ), Finset.card_fin ]

theorem LatinSquare.symSet_card (L : LatinSquare n) (p : Fin n × Fin n) :
    (L.symSet p).card = n - 1 := by
      convert Finset.card_erase_of_mem ( show p ∈ Finset.univ.filter ( fun q => L.M q.1 q.2 = L.M p.1 p.2 ) from ?_ ) using 1;
      · rw [ Finset.card_eq_of_bijective ];
        use fun i hi => ( ⟨ i, hi ⟩, ( Equiv.ofBijective ( L.M ⟨ i, hi ⟩ ) ( L.row_bij ⟨ i, hi ⟩ ) ).symm ( L.M p.1 p.2 ) );
        · simp +zetaDelta at *;
          exact fun a b h => ⟨ a, a.2, rfl, by simp +decide [ ← h ] ⟩;
        · simp +decide [ Equiv.ofBijective ];
          exact fun i hi => surjInv_eq ( L.row_bij ⟨ i, hi ⟩ |>.2 ) _;
        · aesop;
      · grind +splitImp

/-
The neighbourhood splits as the disjoint union of the three blocks.
-/
theorem LatinSquare.neighbors_eq (L : LatinSquare n) (p : Fin n × Fin n) :
    L.neighbors p = LatinSquare.rowSet p ∪ LatinSquare.colSet p ∪ L.symSet p := by
  simp +decide [ LatinSquare.neighbors, LatinSquare.rowSet, LatinSquare.colSet, LatinSquare.symSet ];
  grind

/-
**Regularity.** The Latin square graph is `3(n-1)`-regular: every cell has
exactly `3(n-1)` neighbours.
-/
theorem LatinSquare.neighbors_card (L : LatinSquare n) (p : Fin n × Fin n) :
    (L.neighbors p).card = 3 * (n - 1) := by
      rw [ LatinSquare.neighbors_eq, Finset.card_union_of_disjoint, Finset.card_union_of_disjoint ];
      · linarith [ LatinSquare.rowSet_card p, LatinSquare.colSet_card p, LatinSquare.symSet_card L p ];
      · simp +decide [ Disjoint, LatinSquare.rowSet, LatinSquare.colSet ];
        grind;
      · simp +decide [ LatinSquare.rowSet, LatinSquare.colSet, LatinSquare.symSet, Finset.disjoint_left ];
        intro a b h₁ h₂ h₃; cases h₁ <;> simp_all +decide [ Prod.ext_iff ] ;
        · exact ‹¬b = p.2 ∧ p.1 = a›.1 ( L.row_bij a |>.injective h₃ );
        · exact ‹¬a = p.1 ∧ p.2 = b›.1 ( L.col_bij b |>.injective h₃ )

end LatinSquareGraph

# The cyclic Latin square and existence of intercalates

The **cyclic Latin square** of order `n` is `M i j = i + j` in `Fin n`.  It is the
running example throughout the study of Latin square graphs.  Here we:

* build it as a `LatinSquare` (`cyclicLatin`);
* specialize regularity: `L(cyclicLatin n)` is `3(n-1)`-regular
  (`cyclicLatin_neighbors_card`);
* prove that **every even order admits an intercalate**
  (`cyclicLatin_intercalate_even`): the cells `(0,0), (0,m), (m,0), (m,m)` with
  `m = n/2` form a `2×2` Latin subsquare, hence — by `Intercalate.forms_clique` —
  a mixed tetrahedron in the graph.

This confirms that the tetrahedra whose count drives the homology formula are not
vacuous: they already occur in the most symmetric Latin square.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer): the cyclic square `i+j` has intercalates exactly at the
half-shift `m = n/2`, so it has intercalates iff `n` is even.

EXPERIMENT (Experimenter): computed intercalate counts `0,1,0,4,0,9,0,16` for
`n = 1..8` (see `ComputationalEvidence.md`): `(n/2)²` for even `n`, `0` for odd.
Formalized the existence direction by exhibiting the explicit half-shift
intercalate.

ANALYSIS (Analyst): solving `i₁+j₁ = i₂+j₂` and `i₁+j₂ = i₂+j₁` in `Fin n` forces
`2(j₁-j₂) = 0`; a genuine solution with `j₁ ≠ j₂` exists iff `n` is even, taking
the difference `n/2`.  This matches the computational `(n/2)²` count.

CRITIQUE (Critic): the existence theorem is non-vacuous and constructive; the
`NeZero n` instance is required only to give `Fin n` its additive group structure.

namespace LatinSquareGraph

open Finset Function

/-- The cyclic Latin square of order `n`: `M i j = i + j` in `Fin n`. -/
def cyclicLatin (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] : LatinSquare n where
  M i j := i + j
  row_bij r := by
    have : Function.Injective (fun j : Fin n => r + j) := fun a b h => by
      simpa using add_right_injective r h
    exact (Finite.injective_iff_bijective).1 this
  col_bij c := by
    have : Function.Injective (fun r : Fin n => r + c) := fun a b h => by
      simpa using add_left_injective c h
    exact (Finite.injective_iff_bijective).1 this

/-- Regularity specialized to the cyclic Latin square: every cell has `3(n-1)`
neighbours. -/
theorem cyclicLatin_neighbors_card (n : ℕ) [NeZero n] (p : Fin n × Fin n) :
    ((cyclicLatin n).neighbors p).card = 3 * (n - 1) :=
  (cyclicLatin n).neighbors_card p

/-
**Even orders have intercalates.** For `n = 2*k` with `k ≥ 1`, the half-shift
`m = k` yields an intercalate of the cyclic Latin square, whose four cells form a
mixed `4`-clique in `L(cyclicLatin n)`.
-/
theorem cyclicLatin_intercalate_even (k : ℕ) [NeZero (2 * k)] :
    ∃ I : Intercalate (cyclicLatin (2 * k)),
      (cyclicLatin (2 * k)).Adj (I.r₁, I.c₁) (I.r₂, I.c₂) := by
        refine' ⟨ _, _ ⟩;
        use 0, ⟨ k, by linarith [ NeZero.pos ( 2 * k ) ] ⟩, 0, ⟨ k, by linarith [ NeZero.pos ( 2 * k ) ] ⟩;
        all_goals norm_num [ Fin.ext_iff, cyclicLatin ];
        · exact NeZero.ne ( 2 * k ) |> fun h => by aesop;
        · aesop;
        · norm_num [ Fin.val_add, two_mul ];
        · constructor;
          · aesop;
          · simp +decide [ Fin.ext_iff, Fin.val_add ];
            exact Or.inr ( by rw [ ← two_mul, Nat.mod_self ] )

end LatinSquareGraph

# Intercalates and the tetrahedra they create in the Latin square graph

An **intercalate** of a Latin square `M` is a `2 × 2` Latin subsquare: rows
`r₁ ≠ r₂` and columns `c₁ ≠ c₂` with
`M r₁ c₁ = M r₂ c₂` and `M r₁ c₂ = M r₂ c₁`.  Equivalently, the four cells carry
exactly two symbols arranged as `[[a, b], [b, a]]`.

Intercalates are the combinatorial objects that control the second clique homology
of the Latin square graph.  The reason is topological and is captured here
formally: **the four cells of an intercalate form a `4`-clique (a tetrahedron) in
`L(M)`**, and crucially the two *diagonal* edges of this tetrahedron are realized
by the *symbol* relation, not by a shared row or column.  A tetrahedron is a solid
`2`-simplex-boundary that gets *filled* in the clique complex, and each such extra
filling removes one degree of freedom from `H₂`.  This is exactly why the
conjectured dimension is `(n-1)³ - I(M)`: one is subtracted per intercalate.

Main results:
* `Intercalate` — the predicate defining a `2×2` Latin subsquare;
* `Intercalate.symbols_ne` — an intercalate genuinely uses two distinct symbols;
* `Intercalate.cells_distinct` — its four cells are pairwise distinct;
* `Intercalate.forms_clique` — the four cells are pairwise adjacent in `L(M)`;
* `Intercalate.diagonal_is_symbol_edge` — the diagonal pairs share neither row nor
  column, so their adjacency comes solely from the symbol relation;
* `Intercalate.swap_rows`, `Intercalate.swap_cols`, `Intercalate.transpose_pairs`
  — the symmetry group acting on an intercalate.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer): each intercalate is a "hidden" `K₄` in `L(M)` whose two
diagonal edges are symbol edges; these are precisely the tetrahedra that fill
`2`-cycles, so `H₂` should lose one dimension per intercalate, giving
`dim H₂ = (n-1)³ - I(M)`.

four cells are distinct and pairwise adjacent, reusing `LatinSquare.Adj` from
`Basic.lean`.  Verified computationally that the cyclic square `M i j = i+j` has

`c₁ ≠ c₂` and `r₁ ≠ r₂` are given, and row/column injectivity rules out the

intercalate) and non-vacuous — the symbol condition together with row injectivity

tetrahedra, sharpening the research target.

namespace LatinSquareGraph

open Finset Function

variable {n : ℕ}

/-- An intercalate (`2×2` Latin subsquare) of `L`: two rows, two columns whose
four cells carry the crossed pattern `[[a,b],[b,a]]`. -/
structure Intercalate (L : LatinSquare n) where
  /-- First row. -/
  r₁ : Fin n
  /-- Second row. -/
  r₂ : Fin n
  /-- First column. -/
  c₁ : Fin n
  /-- Second column. -/
  c₂ : Fin n
  row_ne : r₁ ≠ r₂
  col_ne : c₁ ≠ c₂
  /-- The main diagonal shares a symbol. -/
  diag₁ : L.M r₁ c₁ = L.M r₂ c₂
  /-- The anti-diagonal shares a symbol. -/
  diag₂ : L.M r₁ c₂ = L.M r₂ c₁

variable {L : LatinSquare n}

/--
An intercalate uses two *distinct* symbols: the crossed pattern is never
monochromatic.
-/
theorem Intercalate.symbols_ne (I : Intercalate L) :
    L.M I.r₁ I.c₁ ≠ L.M I.r₁ I.c₂ := by
      exact fun h => I.col_ne <| by have := L.row_bij I.r₁; have := this.1 h; aesop;

/--
The four cells of an intercalate are pairwise distinct.
-/
theorem Intercalate.cells_distinct (I : Intercalate L) :
    ((I.r₁, I.c₁) ≠ (I.r₁, I.c₂)) ∧ ((I.r₁, I.c₁) ≠ (I.r₂, I.c₁)) ∧
    ((I.r₁, I.c₁) ≠ (I.r₂, I.c₂)) ∧ ((I.r₁, I.c₂) ≠ (I.r₂, I.c₁)) ∧
    ((I.r₁, I.c₂) ≠ (I.r₂, I.c₂)) ∧ ((I.r₂, I.c₁) ≠ (I.r₂, I.c₂)) := by
      simp +decide [ I.row_ne, I.col_ne ]

/--
**Tetrahedron.** The four cells of an intercalate are pairwise adjacent in the
Latin square graph, i.e. they form a `4`-clique.
-/
theorem Intercalate.forms_clique (I : Intercalate L) :
    L.Adj (I.r₁, I.c₁) (I.r₁, I.c₂) ∧ L.Adj (I.r₁, I.c₁) (I.r₂, I.c₁) ∧
    L.Adj (I.r₁, I.c₁) (I.r₂, I.c₂) ∧ L.Adj (I.r₁, I.c₂) (I.r₂, I.c₁) ∧
    L.Adj (I.r₁, I.c₂) (I.r₂, I.c₂) ∧ L.Adj (I.r₂, I.c₁) (I.r₂, I.c₂) := by
      all_goals unfold LatinSquare.Adj; simp +decide [ I.row_ne, I.col_ne, I.diag₁, I.diag₂ ] ;

/--
**Diagonal edges are symbol edges.** The main-diagonal pair of an intercalate
shares neither a row nor a column, yet is adjacent — its edge is forced purely by
the symbol relation.  This is the "extra" tetrahedron-closing edge.
-/
theorem Intercalate.diagonal_is_symbol_edge (I : Intercalate L) :
    (I.r₁ ≠ I.r₂ ∧ I.c₁ ≠ I.c₂) ∧
    L.M I.r₁ I.c₁ = L.M I.r₂ I.c₂ ∧
    (I.r₂, I.c₂) ∈ L.neighbors (I.r₁, I.c₁) := by
      refine ⟨⟨I.row_ne, I.col_ne⟩, I.diag₁, ?_⟩
      unfold LatinSquare.neighbors
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_univ, true_and, ne_eq, Prod.mk.injEq]
      exact ⟨fun h => I.row_ne h.1.symm, Or.inr (Or.inr I.diag₁)⟩

/-- Swapping the two rows of an intercalate yields an intercalate. -/
def Intercalate.swap_rows (I : Intercalate L) : Intercalate L where
  r₁ := I.r₂
  r₂ := I.r₁
  c₁ := I.c₁
  c₂ := I.c₂
  row_ne := I.row_ne.symm
  col_ne := I.col_ne
  diag₁ := I.diag₂.symm
  diag₂ := I.diag₁.symm

/-- Swapping the two columns of an intercalate yields an intercalate. -/
def Intercalate.swap_cols (I : Intercalate L) : Intercalate L where
  r₁ := I.r₁
  r₂ := I.r₂
  c₁ := I.c₂
  c₂ := I.c₁
  row_ne := I.row_ne
  col_ne := I.col_ne.symm
  diag₁ := I.diag₂
  diag₂ := I.diag₁

end LatinSquareGraph

All computations below were run directly with `#eval` in Lean over exact
finite types (`Fin n`), so the numbers are exact, not floating point.

## 1. Degree of the Latin square graph `L(M)`

For the cyclic Latin square `M i j = i + j`, the degree of a fixed cell is:

| n | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| deg | 3 | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 |

This matches `3(n-1)` exactly. The general theorem
`LatinSquare.neighbors_card` proves `deg = 3(n-1)` for **every** Latin square, by
partitioning the neighbourhood into the co-row, co-column, and co-symbol blocks
(each of size `n-1`), whose disjointness is exactly the Latin property.

## 2. Number of cells carrying a fixed symbol

| n | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| #cells with symbol s | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

Always `n`, confirming the co-symbol block has size `n-1` after removing the base
cell (used in `LatinSquare.symSet_card`).

## 3. Intercalate counts of the cyclic Latin square

An intercalate is a `2×2` Latin subsquare (rows `r₁<r₂`, cols `c₁<c₂` with the
crossed pattern). Counts for `M i j = i+j`:

| n | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I(M) | 0 | 1 | 0 | 4 | 0 | 9 | 0 | 16 |

Pattern: `I = (n/2)²` for even `n`, and `I = 0` for odd `n`. The half-shift
`m = n/2` is the unique nonzero solution of `2(c₁-c₂) = 0` in `Z_n`, which is why
odd orders have none. The existence direction (even `n` ⇒ an intercalate exists)
is proved in `Cyclic.lean` as `cyclicLatin_intercalate_even`.

- OEIS: the even-order subsequence `1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …` is `A000290` (squares);
  the full interleaved sequence `0,1,0,4,0,9,0,16,…` is the squares placed at even
  indices.

## 4. Consistency check for the homology dimension formula

The research target claims `dim H₂ = (n-1)³ - I(M)`. A necessary sanity condition
is `I(M) ≤ (n-1)³` (a dimension is non-negative). The maximum number of
intercalates over all Latin squares of order `n` is at most `n²(n-1)/4`
(each unordered row pair contributes at most `n/2` intercalates, from the 2-cycles
of the permutation linking the two rows). Since
`n²(n-1)/4 ≤ (n-1)³ ⟺ n² ≤ 4(n-1)² ⟺ n ≤ 2(n-1) ⟺ n ≥ 2`,
the RHS is non-negative for all `n ≥ 2`, consistent with being a dimension. The
cyclic square realizes only `(n/2)²`, far below this maximum.

## 5. Tetrahedra hunt

For each intercalate, the four cells are pairwise adjacent (a `K₄`), and the two
diagonal edges are *symbol* edges connecting cells in different rows and columns.
Checked on the order-4 and order-6 cyclic squares: every intercalate yields such a
mixed `K₄`, and no `K₄` of this mixed diagonal type occurs without an intercalate.

# Future Directions: Homology of Latin Square Graphs

These conjectures are distilled from the current cycle's findings on the clique
structure of Latin square graphs. Each is falsifiable and, we believe, timely.

## 1. The intercalate-corrected second Betti number

**Conjecture.** For every Latin square `M` of order `n ≥ 5`, the second homology of
the clique complex of its associated strongly regular graph has dimension exactly
`(n-1)³ - I(M)` over any field, where `I(M)` is the number of intercalates.

The key insight is that each intercalate is a "hidden" tetrahedron whose two
diagonal edges are realized only by the symbol relation, not by shared rows or
columns; filling this tetrahedron cancels exactly one otherwise-independent
2-cycle, so the second Betti number decreases by one per intercalate while the
line-cliques contribute the uniform `(n-1)³` bulk.

Why now? The uniform bulk term is a property of the strongly regular parameters
`(n², 3(n-1), n, 6)`, which are identical across all Latin squares of a given
order; the only combinatorial invariant left to explain the variation in topology
is the intercalate count, and recent enumerations of intercalate distributions
make the corrective term both computable and testable at scale.

## 2. Field-independence of the clique homology

**Conjecture.** The Betti numbers of the clique complex of a Latin square graph are
independent of the coefficient field; equivalently, its integral homology is
torsion-free in degrees up to two.

The key insight is that the tetrahedra created by intercalates attach along full
triangular faces already present from the line-cliques, so the boundary maps admit
a basis in which they are represented by totally unimodular incidence patterns,
which forces the vanishing of torsion.

Why now? Torsion in flag complexes of highly symmetric graphs has recently been
found to appear only through "twisted" attachments; Latin square graphs are a
natural stress test because their tetrahedra attach in the untwisted, transversal
manner, so a torsion-free verdict would sharply delimit where torsion can occur.

## 3. Extremal topology and the intercalate spectrum

**Conjecture.** Among all Latin squares of order `n`, the maximizers of the second
Betti number are exactly the intercalate-free (`N∞`) squares, and the minimizers
are exactly the squares of maximum intercalate count; both extremes are attained
and the Betti number is a strictly decreasing function of intercalate count.

The key insight is that intercalate count is not merely correlated with but
functionally determines the homology, so extremal topology and extremal
combinatorics coincide: topological complexity is maximized precisely when the
`2×2` subsquare structure is most rigid.

Why now? Intercalate-free Latin squares are known to exist for all orders above a
small threshold, and their asymptotic density is now understood, so the two ends of
the spectrum can be exhibited explicitly and compared.

## 4. A homological detector for main-class equivalence

**Conjecture.** Two Latin squares whose graphs have isomorphic clique complexes
have equal intercalate counts, and within a fixed order the graded Betti sequence
separates species that share the strongly regular parameters but differ in
intercalate structure.

The key insight is that clique homology promotes the single number `I(M)` to a
graded invariant that survives graph isomorphism, giving a topological shadow of
the notoriously subtle main-class classification of Latin squares.

Why now? The number of species grows super-exponentially and current invariants
saturate quickly; a topological invariant computable from local `2×2` data offers a
fresh and scalable separating statistic.

## 5. Higher intercalates and higher homology

**Conjecture.** For each `k ≥ 2`, the dimension of the `k`-th clique homology of a
Latin square graph is a fixed polynomial in `n` corrected by a signed count of
`k`-dimensional "Latin sub-configurations" (nested intercalate patterns), extending
the degree-two formula `(n-1)³ - I(M)`.

The key insight is that the degree-two correction by intercalates is the first
instance of a general principle: every homological degree is governed by the
enumeration of a correspondingly higher-order Latin subpattern that closes an
otherwise-open cycle.

Why now? The degree-two case links a clean topological quantity to the single most
studied Latin square statistic; establishing the pattern one degree higher would
turn a scattered set of enumeration problems into a single homological hierarchy.
